planting.note: Start seed under lights in late winter on the surface of a fine, moist mix, or begin dormant tubers concave-side up in shallow trays in late winter; Avanti is bred as an early-flowering F1 series for pot production and blooms faster from seed than open-pollinated gloxinia strains.

directions: Avanti is a compact, early-blooming gloxinia series bred for uniform pot production, forming a tight rosette of broad, velvety leaves topped with large, upward-facing, single trumpet flowers in solid purple, red, magenta, or white. Grow in bright indirect light near an east or north window; direct sun scorches the fuzzy foliage while too little light stalls flowering. Water from below or around the crown to keep moisture off the leaves, which spot readily, and let the surface dry slightly between waterings. Compared to older open-pollinated gloxinia strains, Avanti flowers noticeably sooner from seed and holds a neater, more compact rosette, making it well suited to windowsill culture in a smaller pot.
sources: Ball Horticultural Company — Gloxinia Avanti series
Muller Seeds — Sinningia speciosa Avanti Mix

planting.note: Surface-sow fine seed on moist mix under lights in late winter, or start dormant tubers concave-side up in shallow trays; Brocade is grown as a flowering pot plant and is typically timed to bloom roughly four months after sowing.

directions: The Brocade series is grown for its heavy flower count and distinctive white-picotee edging on many of its flared, trumpet-shaped blooms, set against dark green, quilted foliage in a dense rosette. Colors range from deep red and burgundy through blue, violet, and rose, with the white margin giving each flower a two-toned, brocaded look. Provide bright, indirect light and avoid wetting the leaves when watering, since standing moisture on the fuzzy foliage encourages spotting and rot; water at the pot edge or from a saucer instead. After bloom, gradually withhold water to let the plant go dormant and store the tuber dry and cool until the next growing season.
sources: Ball Horticultural Company — Gloxinia Brocade series
Muller Seeds — Sinningia speciosa Brocade Mix

planting.note: Surface-sow fine seed on moist mix under lights, or start dormant tubers concave-side up in shallow trays in late winter; Empress is a large-flowered gift-plant series grown for gallon-pot production and holiday or spring flowering.

directions: Empress is a large-flowered gloxinia series bred for gift-plant production, producing extra-large, velvety trumpet blooms in saturated jewel tones — deep purple with a spotted throat, solid red, and other rich shades — held above a full rosette of dark, hairy leaves. Grow in bright indirect light and keep water off the foliage, watering instead at the soil surface or by setting the pot in a shallow saucer briefly. The heavier flower size means Empress benefits from slightly more room and a sturdier pot than compact series like Avanti. Let the plant dry down and go dormant after its bloom flush, then rest the tuber dry and cool before restarting it the following spring.
sources: Ferry-Morse / Ferri Seeds — Gloxinia Empress Mix
Royal Horticultural Society — Sinningia speciosa Empress Purple Spotted AGM

planting.note: Start from a tiny pea-sized tuber or leaf cutting in a covered terrarium or humid propagation tray on a light, well-drained mix; S. concinna is fussier about humidity than S. pusilla and grows best enclosed rather than on an open windowsill.

directions: A stemless miniature rosette species similar in scale to S. pusilla but with rosier pink flowers and, in most forms, decorative purple spotting in the throat. It grows from a tiny persistent tuber and is best kept enclosed in a terrarium or bottle garden, since it wants steady humidity above 50 percent and sulks in the drier air of an open room. Provide bright, indirect or artificial light, a light peat-perlite mix that drains quickly, and even moisture without letting water pool around the crown. S. concinna is more difficult to grow to flowering size and slower to set seed than S. pusilla, but it has been used as a parent of many popular miniature sinningia hybrids, passing on its compact form and spotted throat.
sources: American Gesneriad Society — miniature Sinningia culture

planting.note: Root a stolon plantlet or stem-tip cutting in moist perlite or a light peat-based mix, then pot up into a shallow, wide container once rooted. Best started in spring or summer so the trailing runners fill in before lower-light winter months.

directions: Pink Panther carries bronze-green, quilted leaves overlaid with a mosaic of silvery-pink veining, with small orange-red flowers that take a back seat to the foliage display. Compared with the more heavily silvered 'Silver Skies' or the near-solid bronze of the plain species, Pink Panther shows a distinct pink cast running through the leaf centers. Grow in bright, indirect light to bring out the pink tones without scorching the leaves, and keep water off the foliage since standing droplets cause spotting on the velvety surface — water at the soil line or set the pot briefly in a saucer. It tolerates slightly lower humidity than many episcias, making it a forgiving choice for hanging baskets outside an enclosed terrarium.
sources: Gesneriad Reference Web — Episcia cupreata 'Pink Panther'

planting.note: Root 4-6 inch stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or a light peat-bark mix, then move to a hanging basket once new growth shows. Best propagated in spring or summer for full establishment before winter.

directions: One of the best-known Columnea hybrids, Early Bird produces slender trailing stems set with small, glossy, dark green leaves and a heavy early flush of orange-red, tubular goldfish-shaped flowers that open well ahead of many other Columnea cultivars in the growing season. Grow in bright, indirect light, since flower count drops sharply in low light even though the trailing foliage stays healthy. Pot in a chunky, fast-draining epiphytic mix and let the surface dry between waterings, keeping water off the leaves to avoid spotting. Display in a hanging basket where the long stems can cascade freely, and pinch tips after flowering to keep growth dense rather than sparse and leggy.

planting.note: Root 4-6 inch stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or a light peat-bark mix, then move to a hanging basket once new growth shows. Best propagated in spring or summer for full establishment before winter.

directions: Grown mainly for its foliage, Aladdin's Lamp carries trailing stems of glossy leaves so dark a purple-black that they read as nearly black against bright red, tubular flowers — a sharper foliage-to-flower contrast than the plain green-leaved Columnea hybrids. Provide bright, indirect light to keep the dark pigment intense, since low light shifts the leaves back toward ordinary green. Pot in a chunky, fast-draining epiphytic mix of bark and perlite, water thoroughly, then allow the surface to dry before watering again, keeping moisture off the foliage. Best displayed in a hanging basket where its trailing habit and near-black leaves can be seen from below and the side.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Finder — Columnea 'Aladdin's Lamp'

planting.note: Root 3-4 inch stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or a light mix, then transplant into a hanging basket once rooted. Best started in spring or summer so trailing stems fill in before the heaviest midwinter bloom flush.

directions: Christmas Holly earns its name from small, very glossy, dark green leaves that resemble holly foliage, paired with pumpkin-orange, pouch-shaped flowers that peak in a heavy midwinter flush rather than blooming evenly year-round like some Nematanthus cultivars. Grow in bright, indirect light for the heaviest bloom set; the thick, waxy leaves tolerate brief dry spells but color and flower production suffer in dim rooms. Pot in a light, fast-draining mix and let the top inch dry between waterings, keeping water off the leaves. Its dense, mounding habit and glossy foliage make it a good hanging-basket companion to plainer green-leaved Nematanthus cultivars, with the holly-like leaf shine as its main distinguishing trait.

planting.note: Root 4-6 inch stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or a light peat-based mix, then move to a hanging basket once new growth shows. Best propagated in spring or summer for full establishment before winter.

directions: Twister arose as a branch mutation of the cultivar 'Rasta' and carries the same tightly curled foliage in a more compact form, with smaller leaves that coil inward and back on themselves to give the trailing stems a corkscrew texture. It flowers less reliably than plain-leaved Aeschynanthus cultivars, with the curled, glossy foliage doing most of the ornamental work, though it can still produce the typical red, tubular lipstick blooms from dark calyces. Grow in bright, indirect light to keep the curl tight and the leaf color deep, and pot in a chunky, fast-draining epiphytic mix, watering thoroughly and then letting the surface dry before watering again. Its more compact size and tighter leaf curl distinguish it from its parent, 'Rasta'.
sources: JOMO Studio — Lipstick Plant Twister care guide

planting.note: Root 4-6 inch stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or a light peat-based mix, then move to a hanging basket once new growth shows. Best propagated in spring or summer for full establishment before winter.

directions: Rasta is grown for its densely twisted, glossy leaves that spiral along the trailing stems in a texture often compared to a Hoya compacta, quite unlike the flat foliage of most Aeschynanthus cultivars. It still produces the genus's characteristic bright red, tubular flowers from dark calyces, typically in the heaviest flush during late summer and early fall, and tolerates lower light and drier air better than many lipstick plant cultivars. Grow in bright, indirect light for the best leaf curl and steadiest bloom, in a chunky, fast-draining epiphytic mix; water thoroughly and let the surface dry before watering again. It is the parent of the more compact 'Twister' sport, which has an even tighter curl and smaller leaves.

planting.note: Divide scaly rhizomes in spring and plant just under the surface of a well-draining, humus-rich mix; stem cuttings also root readily in a light medium. Grow as a year-round houseplant, since Kohleria cannot tolerate frost.

directions: Longwood is a vigorous, upright hybrid believed to be a relic of old Kohleria breeding lines, rediscovered growing in a botanical garden and reintroduced through Longwood Gardens. It is a taller grower than the species, reaching a foot and a half, with soft, hairy, dark green leaves and brilliant strawberry-red, tubular flowers with a white throat that appear almost continuously rather than in distinct flushes. Grow in bright indirect light, and pot in a well-draining, slightly acidic mix, allowing the surface to approach dryness between waterings since the scaly rhizomes are prone to rot in soggy soil. Keep water off the fuzzy foliage to prevent spotting. Its outstanding vigor and near-continuous bloom set it apart from more seasonal-flowering Kohleria cultivars.

planting.note: Divide scaly rhizomes in spring and plant just under the surface of a well-draining, humus-rich mix; stem cuttings also root readily. Its compact habit makes it well suited to growing under fluorescent or LED plant lights year-round.

directions: A relatively small-growing, floriferous Kohleria hybrid registered with the Gesneriad Society, bred compact enough to thrive under artificial lights where taller Kohleria cultivars sprawl out of bounds. Soft, hairy leaves cover the upright stems, and reddish-pink, tubular flowers are held well above the foliage rather than tucked among the leaves, giving a cleaner floral display than many rhizomatous gesneriads. Grow in bright indirect or fluorescent light, and pot in a well-draining, slightly acidic mix, letting the surface approach dryness between waterings to protect the scaly rhizomes from rot. Keep water off the fuzzy leaves to avoid spotting. Its compact scale distinguishes it from taller Kohleria hybrids such as 'Longwood'.
sources: Gesneriad Society Cultivar Registry — Kohleria 'Strawberry Fields'

planting.note: Divide offsets from the basal rosette or root individual leaf cuttings in a light, well-draining mix; grow as a year-round houseplant, since Primulina cannot tolerate frost and is easily damaged by cold, wet soil.

directions: A compact Primulina cultivar registered with the Gesneriad Society and noted among hobbyists as one of the smallest-growing named forms in the genus, forming a tight, symmetrical rosette of thick, textured leaves well suited to windowsill or under-light collections where larger primulinas outgrow their space. Slender stalks carry small tubular flowers above the foliage on an intermittent bloom cycle. Grow in bright, indirect light and a fast-draining, mineral-rich mix, watering around the base of the rosette rather than over the leaves, since standing moisture on the thick foliage invites rot. Like other former Chirita relatives, it prefers slightly drier conditions between waterings than true African violets.
sources: The Violet Barn — Primulina culture notes
